title: The Examined Life
logline: First week of classes: a famous atheist demands proof of a soul, a harbor diner needs a dishwasher, and the girl from the porch turns out to be the other half of the assignment.

previously.text: Your father drove you 2,400 miles and saw the Pacific for the first time.
On the back porch of the Lighthouse, a girl from New Orleans judged a party with you — and then judged you.
She took the cigarette out of your mouth and kept it.
At Mass she wore a mantilla. Afterward you argued about lip service, and you won.
On the stairwell she told someone named Wes she loved him. Then she told him you were nobody.
Adrian Hale emailed the seminar: come prepared to prove you have a soul. You hit Reply All.

s01.slug: MONDAY · 3:07 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LAWN BY THE LAGOON
body: The alarm doesn’t ring so much as happen to the building: a horn like a goose being audited, a strobe stuttering in every hallway, and three hundred and ten freshmen pouring down the stairwells in whatever they sleep in. Out on the lawn, Delgado blinks white over the Lagoon like a ship in trouble. Fog to the knees. The eucalyptus drips on everybody with real commitment, and the grass squeaks.
Jack is barefoot, in basketball shorts and the gray Cardinal Mooney hoodie, the RAZR in his fist out of pure habit. It buzzes.

body: On the lobby steps Priya, in a Fremont High hoodie, uses the air horn for the first time in recorded history — one flat, enormous blast — and three hundred people shut up. A fresh laminate is taped to the glass door behind her: COVER YOUR COUGH. H1N1 DOES NOT CARE ABOUT YOUR FEELINGS. “FOURTH FLOOR! PRUITT! TRAN! VANCE! *COSTIGAN!*” Kevin Tran is at her elbow with a second clipboard, quarter-zip zipped to the sternum at three in the morning. Nobody has to tell Jack he volunteered.
“*Costigan*,” says a Texan voice twenty feet off, trying it on. “Like a cop show.”

The floor, in its natural habitat. Margot, fully dressed in black down to the Docs and visibly not cold, writing in her Moleskine by strobe light; she turns the page to show him — ALARM 1., underlined. “I’m establishing a baseline.” Theo in a navy silk robe, carrying the espresso machine like an infant out of a burning village. “I saved what mattered.” And last out of the building, Doug Pruitt: barefoot, out the fire door at the far east end, the wrong end of the hall from 420, with a pillow under his arm like a football. He looks down at the pillow as if somebody handed it to him on the way out.

The cop-show voice is Laney: sleep mask pushed up into her copper hair like a tiara, pearls, a camisole, and over it an oatmeal cardigan with holes at the elbows that Jack last saw on a porch. She throws both arms up. “My *fireman*.”

Beside her, arms crossed hard against the cold, is Lena: a faded black Saints T-shirt, the fleur-de-lis cracked from washing and WHO DAT across the chest, pajama pants, Keds with the laces dragging in the wet, her hair in a knot she clearly did in the dark and hasn’t forgiven.
“Youngstown,” she says.
“Broussard.”

Theo materializes at his shoulder, machine and all. “*Broussard*. *M.* Broussard. In the flesh.” Lena takes in the robe, the machine, the hair. “And you are?” “The roommate. I dared him.” “Then I blame you.” Theo turns to Jack and doesn’t lower his voice at all. “I like her. She’s mean.”

journal.title: Fire alarm, 3:07 a.m.
journal.text: Everybody on the lawn in what they sleep in. Theo saved the espresso machine. Margot wrote ‘ALARM 1’ like it was a case number.

choices.text: “Some of us read the syllabus in July.”
response: She doesn’t miss a step. “Some of us read it *twice*. Bring a pen, Youngstown. I’ve seen your margins.” She has, on the porch, for most of an hour. Laney leans in like she’s passing a stock tip. “She has a highlighter system. It’s color-coded by *sin*.”
At 3:31 the strobes die and three hundred and ten people squeak back inside. Lena takes the east stairs two at a time and doesn’t look back. On the second-floor landing, she does.

choices.text: Pull off the Mooney hoodie and hold it out to her.
response: He’s out of it before he’s thought about it. Lena doesn’t take it. “I’ve got a cardigan. Laney’s wearing it.” Laney takes the hoodie instead and is inside it before anybody can object. It comes to her knees. She reads CARDINAL MOONEY upside down off her own chest and declares herself a cardinal. Jack stands there in a Browns T-shirt, getting rained on by a tree. Lena watches him be cold and says nothing about it, and the nothing carries.

At 3:31 the strobes die and three hundred and ten people squeak back inside, Jack in his T-shirt with his arms wrapped around himself. Lena takes the east stairs two at a time and doesn’t look back. On the second-floor landing, she does.

choices.text: “How were the red beans?”
response: For half a second she’s slower than he has ever seen her, and he’d bet she’s finding the Anchor in it. Then: “Somebody had to feed this building.” Laney groans into the cardigan collar. “She made a *vat*. At eleven p.m. On a *Sunday*. The whole second floor smells like a Baptist potluck.”
At 3:31 the strobes die and three hundred and ten people squeak back inside. Lena takes the east stairs two at a time and doesn’t look back. On the second-floor landing, she does.

choices.text: “How’s Archbishop?”
response: She laughs before she can stop it, a short undignified honk into the fog, and claps a hand over it, furious — at him, at the laugh, at the hour. “Pray for him. He confirmed a child.” Theo looks from one to the other. “Who’s Archbishop?” “Nobody,” they say together. Theo looks like a man who has found a conspiracy and means to be inside it by breakfast.
At 3:31 the strobes die and three hundred and ten people squeak back inside. Lena takes the east stairs two at a time and doesn’t look back. On the second-floor landing, she does.

body: By noon the fog has burned off as if it had never been invented. The cloister walk along Hollis is red tile and arches, the bougainvillea dropping magenta faster than anybody could sweep it. Room 302: a long oak table scarred with other people’s initials, twelve chairs, a radiator that knocks in September for no reason anyone has found, and a window full of sea.

Jack is in the navy Goodwill blazer — a lifeguard at a funeral, per Theo. In his back pocket: Benedict XVI, *Spe Salvi*, the Ignatius edition, thin as a parish pamphlet, two dollars off the cart outside Driftwood Books on Sunday. For a bookmark, a holy card of the man himself, white cassock, both hands raised, a grandfather who has read everything you have and remembers it better.

Lena is already there. Of course she is: the chair at the head’s right hand, a faded green sundress, brown Justins crossed at the ankle, the syllabus annotated in three colors of ink, a fountain pen uncapped beside it like a drawn weapon. Jack takes the chair directly across from her. There is no other chair. There are nine other chairs.

body.title: PHIL 9H · THE EXAMINED LIFE · Prof. A. C. Hale
body.text:
Week 1. Is anybody in there? Descartes, *Meditations* II; Ryle, *The Concept of Mind*, ch. 1; Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* I, qq. 75–76.
Attendance is compulsory. Agreement is not.

body: A boy with a Central Valley twang drops in beside Jack with a Darwin-fish laptop and a copy of *The Consolations of Disbelief* so stuffed with Post-its it looks like it’s molting. “Caleb. Visalia. I’ve read it six times. I’m not proud.” He looks proud.
Jack sets *Spe Salvi* on the oak and the holy card slides half out. Lena’s eyes go to it like a cat’s to a moth. “You carry the Pope in your back pocket. Like a ticket stub.”

“I carry *this* Pope.” He means to stop there, and doesn’t. “Smartest man alive who’s also in charge of anything. Regensburg — best lecture anybody’s given in a university in fifty years, and nobody read past the part they were angry about. And this.” He taps it. “Section two. ‘The one who has hope lives differently.’ He put my whole religion in a sentence and then wrote forty-nine more sections to be polite.”

“I’d follow him into a burning building,” Lena says. “I just wouldn’t put him on my wall. His shoes are Prada.” “That’s a myth. The Vatican paper denied it, in print. They’re papal red. It’s *martyrs’* red.” She stares at him, pen suspended. “Lord. You’ve researched his *shoes*.” Beside him Caleb murmurs “Selah” — by reflex, the way another kid would say *touché* — and looks appalled at himself.

The rest come too fast to learn. A lean kid in a Mission San Jose sweatshirt, no water bottle on a warm day — “Yusuf. Fremont. Aerospace. It’s Ramadan, so if I pass out, put me on my side” — takes in the holy card and the fountain pen and says to nobody, “Oh, good. The Catholics are here.” A Palo Alto girl who has read the whole syllabus and resents everyone who hasn’t. A quiet kid hiding a chemistry textbook. Two lanky boys from San Diego with the same surname, haircut and hoodie, who are not related and are tired of saying so.

At 1:07 Adrian Hale comes in without hurrying, which is louder than hurrying. The linen jacket; the wine on the cuff, the same stain as yesterday, Jack would swear; reading glasses pushed up into the silver hair and forgotten. He sits at the head of the table, sets down nothing, and looks at no one.
“Prove to me you have a soul. You have ninety minutes and I’ve had lunch.”

Then he looks round the table, slowly, chair by chair. “Which of you is Youngstown? No —” His eyes stop on Jack’s left eyebrow. “— there you are. The nine pages. And you replied to *all*, Mr. Costigan. Brave or careless; we’ll find out. Miss Broussard replied to all of us to correct you, which I enjoyed rather more.”

He laces his fingers over his stomach. “We’ve met, the three of us, after a fashion. Yesterday, at the Anchor. A girl who left as though I’d set fire to her coffee, and a boy who went after her like a spaniel. I do love a roster.”
“I’d remembered something I left on the stove,” Lena says evenly, and her hand goes to the gold medal at her throat and closes on it.
Hale lets it go, with open pleasure, the way a man lets a fish run when he’s in no hurry at all. Under the window, the radiator knocks once.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Knew my face from the Anchor before he knew my name. Called me a spaniel.

journal.title: Caleb (PHIL 9H)
journal.text: Visalia. Has Hale’s book with forty Post-its in it. Says ‘Selah’ when he means ‘touché.’

journal.title: Yusuf (PHIL 9H)
journal.text: Fremont. Engineer. Fasting for Ramadan through a ninety-minute seminar and funnier than all of us.

body: Hale doesn’t lecture; he gossips about the dead. “Descartes shut himself in a stove-heated room in Germany one winter and came out with two kinds of stuff: the body, which is a machine, and the mind, which is a ghost inside it pulling the levers. Very tidy. Nobody since has explained how a ghost pulls a lever.”

“Then Ryle, 1949. *The Concept of Mind*. ‘The dogma of the Ghost in the Machine.’ A visitor to Oxford is shown the colleges, the libraries, the playing fields, the laboratories, and at the end of the day he asks: yes, lovely, but where is the *University*?” He spreads his hands. “I spent a decade being the University and never once ran into it. That’s a category mistake, and you make it every time you say *soul*. So. Show me where it’s kept.”

Caleb goes first, Post-its fluttering. “Dennett. *Consciousness Explained*. There’s no theater in the head, no little guy watching the screen —” “Or explained *away*,” Hale murmurs, approving, as if a retriever had come back proudly with the wrong stick.

Yusuf, hands folded on the oak: “I’m fasting, Professor. My soul is the only part of me that isn’t hungry.” The table laughs, and Hale laughs with it, head back, a real laugh with Yorkshire somewhere under the Oxford, and writes it down.

“Nobody at this table believes in your ghost, Professor,” Lena says. “Aquinas says the soul is the *form* of the body. Not a passenger — the shape matter takes because it’s alive. Ryle spent a whole book beating up a Frenchman.”
Hale regards her over the glasses he isn’t wearing. Then he turns, unhurried. “And Youngstown? A ghost man or a form man?”

choices.text: Side with her and push further: the intellect holds *triangle* and *justice*, which no organ can. Aquinas, *ST* I q.75 a.2.
response: “Form,” Jack says. “And she’s underselling it. I can hold *triangle* in my head — not this one or that one — and *justice*, which nobody’s ever weighed. No organ holds a universal. Aquinas, question seventy-five: the intellect has an act of its own. Call it what you like. It isn’t a ghost.”

“Two Thomists,” Hale says. “*Christ*.” Lena doesn’t look at Jack; her pen taps the table twice, which might be applause. “Universals are a grammar, Mr. Costigan, not a ghost. But it was nicely parsed.”

choices.text: “You asked where it’s kept. Same place as your manners, Professor.”
response: “Nobody’s ever seen them,” Jack says, “but we’re assured they exist.” The room goes off like a dropped tray; Caleb laughs and then looks betrayed by it. Hale inclines his head a quarter inch, a fencer conceding the touch. “Ten minutes in and he’s gone for the man. Good. It saves time.”

choices.text: Augustine, *Confessions* X: he went looking inside his own memory and found palaces too big for his head.
response: “Neither. Augustine, *Confessions*, book ten. He goes looking for God in his own memory and gets lost in there — fields, caves, ‘spacious palaces,’ more rooms than any skull could hold. ‘I have become a question to myself.’ You want to know where it’s kept? It’s an inside with no floor plan.”

Hale’s eyebrows rise against what looks like his better judgment. “Rooms. How very Protestant of a Catholic.” Across the table Lena’s head has turned. It isn’t her answer. He watches her draw a neat line through something on her syllabus, in green.

choices.text: “I can’t show you where it’s kept. I can tell you I’ve felt it go missing.”
response: Hale stops. It lasts about one second, which in Hale is a long time. “I can’t do a thing with that, Mr. Costigan.” The radiator knocks. “But it’s the first true thing anybody’s said today.” Lena looks at Jack across the table, a short straight look, and she’s the one who ends it.

body: Hale goes to the window and tells the next part to the Pacific, low and confiding, the way you’d tell a ghost story to children you were fond of.

“Vermont. September 1848. The Rutland and Burlington Railroad is blasting a cut through rock near Cavendish, and the foreman is a capable, well-liked young man named Phineas Gage. He’s tamping powder into a drill hole with an iron bar — three feet seven inches, thirteen and a quarter pounds. The powder goes off.” He turns around. “The bar goes in under his left cheekbone, out through the top of his skull, and lands in the dirt yards behind him, greasy with what used to be the front of his brain.”

The Palo Alto girl makes a small noise. “He sits up in the oxcart. He *talks*. He greets the doctor: ‘Doctor, here is business enough for you.’ He lives. And afterwards —” He comes back to his chair and folds his hands. “His doctor wrote that his friends said he was ‘no longer Gage.’ Fitful. Profane. Impossible. Damage the brain, change the man. A soul that can be knocked out of a man with a railroad spike is not much of a soul.”
Jack’s hand has gone to his left eyebrow. He finds it there, his thumb on the white line, and takes it down and lays it flat on the oak.
The table has gone quiet in a different way. Across from him Lena is looking at his hand, not his face.

choices.text: Smash the piano and you haven’t disproved the pianist. Aquinas got there first: injure the organ and understanding is *impeded*.
response: His voice comes out plainer than he means it to. “You break the piano, you haven’t disproved the pianist. You just don’t get music.” He keeps going. “And Aquinas beat your railroad to it. In this life the intellect works through images, and if the organ of the imagination is hurt, understanding is impeded. He names frenzy. Impeded isn’t gone.”

Hale looks delighted to be handed Aquinas against himself. “A soul that survives every injury by declining to do anything. Marvelous. The perfect civil servant.” Jack’s answer is hanging on by one hand. “Question eighty-four,” Lena says quietly, before he can find it. “Article seven.” He lets her.

choices.text: “Then somebody still had to love whoever Gage was afterward.”
response: It comes out quiet and plain, in a voice he hasn’t used at this table. “Then whoever Gage was afterward, somebody still had to love that guy. His mother didn’t stop. If there was nothing left of him, what was she loving?”

Hale looks at him a while. “Her memory, Mr. Costigan.” And then, unexpectedly: “She didn’t stop, as it happens. He died in her house.” It doesn’t sound like a point for either of them. Across the table, Lena has stopped writing.

choices.text: Afterward Gage drove six-horse stagecoaches over the mountains in Chile. “I’ve seen Browns quarterbacks take less and retire.”
response: It’s a joke, mostly; it just comes out quieter than a joke should. “He went to Chile. Drove a six-horse coach over the mountains for years. I’ve seen Browns quarterbacks take less and retire.” The room laughs, glad to. “There’s a man in Melbourne who’s written an entire book agreeing with you about Chile,” Hale says, “which I find irritating. The Browns I’ll take on faith.”

choices.text: “You were drinking a Bloody Mary at one-thirty on Sunday. When you order the second one, is that you or the vodka?”
response: It comes out cold, which surprises Jack more than anybody. Hale’s smile arrives and stays, delighted and freezing at once. “Both, Mr. Costigan. And the second is always better company.”

Nobody moves. Caleb appears to have stopped breathing. Lena, under her breath, to the oak: “Lord.” Hale writes something in the margin of the roster, beside what Jack has to assume is his name, and doesn’t say what.

body: Hale pours himself water from a carafe nobody saw him bring, regards it with disappointment, and drinks it anyway. Then he sets the two of them on each other.

body.text: “Miss Broussard says the soul is the body’s form. Mr. Costigan has rooms in his. A tenant, then, in a house too big for it.”
“Miss Broussard says the soul is the body’s form. But Mr. Costigan’s goes missing. A thing that can leave is a tenant.”

“Mr. Costigan either agrees with Miss Broussard, which is cowardice, or has been too busy being charming to say, which is worse. Let me help. Mr. Costigan, you’ll defend the tenant — Aquinas lets the soul outlive its body; there’s your lease. Miss Broussard, evict him.” Lena lights up like somebody has tossed her a ball she’s been catching since grade school.

body: “You can’t both be right,” Hale says. “Settle it. I’ll hold your coats.”
Lena turns to face Jack square, and he can see the rematch arrive in her at last. She reaches for cardigan sleeves she isn’t wearing and settles for squaring her syllabus against the oak.

“If the soul’s a tenant, the body’s a rental. And you know what people do with rentals. That’s how you get a whole culture that treats bodies like hotel rooms: check in, trash it, leave the key on the dresser.” This to Hale as much as to Jack. “I have nothing against anybody having a good time in a hotel, Professor. I’m against pretending nobody lives there. If I *am* my body, then what happens to it happens to *me*. Every time.” Back to Jack. “Your tenant’s a Cartesian, Costigan. Evict him or I will.”

choices.text: “Then what survives death? Aquinas needs the soul to subsist on its own. He’s half on my side.”
response: “Then what survives death? Aquinas needs the soul to subsist without the body, or there’s nobody home after the funeral. He’s half on my side.”

She doesn’t let him land. “Subsists *incomplete*. It wants the body back — it’s ‘naturally apt’ for it, his phrase. That’s why it’s the resurrection of the *body*, Costigan. We say so every time we start a rosary.” “Point to the lady,” Hale says. “Rigor to the gentleman. I’m enjoying this far more than my doctor would like.”

choices.text: “She’s right. My side gets you Descartes, and Descartes gets you a body you can rent out.”
response: Lena stops mid-breath. She had three more paragraphs loaded; he could see them stacked behind her teeth. She looks at him as though he’s slid something across the table that she now has to decide whether to keep. “Disappointing,” Hale says. “Do go on, Miss Broussard. He’s given you the floor.” She doesn’t use it right away.

choices.text: “We’re both right, and he’s counting on us not to notice.” Turn on Hale together.
response: “Augustine’s rooms are in Aquinas’s house.” Lena takes it without a hitch — “The interior *is* the form, seen from inside” — and for ninety seconds they don’t fight each other at all: she hands him the *Summa*, he hands her book ten, she finishes his Augustine and he finishes her Aristotle, and Hale watches, chin on his fist, as two freshmen build something at him. “Oh, they’ve formed a *union*.”
Jack thinks, for no reason he could defend in this room, of his father’s Local 1112 jacket on the hook by the back door.

choices.text: “Says the girl who walked out of the Anchor the second she saw a magazine. Was that your soul leaving, or just your body?”
choices.key: You used the Anchor against Lena in front of Hale.
response: It’s out before he’s finished deciding to say it. Lena goes still, and then polite, which is worse than anything she could have thrown. “I’d forgotten something on the stove, Mr. Costigan,” she says pleasantly, and her fingers find the medal at her throat and close on it.

The room’s sympathy comes about and fills on her side of the table like a sail. Hale, very softly: “Ah.” In the quiet Jack hears his own line again and wants it back more than he has wanted most things.

body: Hale takes the glasses down off his head at last and pockets them, and somehow that’s how they know this is the one he came to make. His voice drops. It isn’t unkind, which is the worst of it.

“Every one of you who believes in a soul was told to by somebody who loved you before you could read. Your mother. Your grandmother. A nun with a felt board. That isn’t a proof. It’s an inheritance. Born in Thebes, you’d be on your knees to Zeus. Born in Riyadh — forgive me, Mr. Noorzai —” “You’re forgiven, Professor. It’s Fremont.” “— you’d face east. Your souls are *addresses*. I don’t say it to be cruel. I say it because not one of you chose, and you’re old enough now to notice.”

body.text: Lena answers him without once looking down the table toward Jack.

body: “That’s the genetic fallacy, Professor,” Lena says. “Where a belief comes from says nothing about whether it’s true. They teach it in Lincoln–Douglas. I was thirteen.” “And yet,” Hale says gently, “it’s true of you.” “It’s true of *me*,” Caleb says, too loud, red to the ears. “I got out.”
Nobody answers that. Then, one by one, as rooms do, they look at Jack.

choices.text: Newman: how a belief got into you says nothing about whether it’s true. And Hale got his from somebody too.
choices.key: You told Hale he’d inherited his atheism too.
response: “Newman, *Grammar of Assent*. We believe most things the way you know there’s a coastline in the fog: a thousand small signs converging, not one proof. None of that cares where you first heard it.” Then, because it’s sitting right there: “I’d bet you got your atheism from your father too, Professor. You just got it by kicking.”

Hale stops. He looks at the window for exactly as long as it takes the radiator to knock twice. Then he’s brisk, all at once, a man gathering papers he hasn’t got. “The genetic fallacy cuts both ways. Well done. We’ll bleed it out on Wednesday.”

choices.text: Tell him the truth: at sixteen, after his book, you tried to put it down.
choices.key: You told Hale that when you tried to leave, there was nowhere to go.
response: Jack doesn’t make it clever. He hasn’t got clever in him right now.

“I didn’t get it from my parents,” he says. “I mean, I did. And at sixteen, after your book, I tried to put it down. A whole winter. I did everything right. I stopped going. I read you twice. And there was nowhere to go. Not a feeling — I’m not telling you about a feeling. I looked around for somewhere else to stand, and there wasn’t anywhere.”

Nobody moves. Out the window a gull hangs in the updraft off the cliff without flapping, as if it’s waiting too. When Hale speaks it’s quietly, and not to the room. “‘Lord, to whom shall we go.’ Yes. I know it. I was made to learn it.”
Across the table Lena has gone very still. She isn’t looking at Hale. She’s looking at Jack.

choices.text: “I was born in Youngstown, Professor. If I picked gods by geography, I’d have picked one with weather.”
choices.key: You answered Hale’s best argument with a joke about the weather in Youngstown.
response: The biggest laugh of the afternoon. Yusuf actually applauds, two flat claps, and the San Diego boys high-five across the Palo Alto girl. Hale smiles the book-jacket smile, devastating and unhurried, and says nothing at all, and it takes Jack a second too long to understand that he’s just lost the round.

choices.text: “That’s the best argument you’ve made. I don’t have an answer today.”
choices.key: You admitted Hale had made an argument you couldn’t answer — yet.
response: Hale considers him. “Honesty. How disappointing. Wednesday, then.” But for the rest of the hour there’s something new in how he looks at Jack: the look of a man who has just been handed a real opponent. Under the table Lena’s boot finds his and kicks it, once. A reprimand or a salute; he can’t tell. From her face, she hasn’t decided either.

body.text: Hale looks out at the sea until the quiet in the room starts to belong to it. Then he caps his pen. “Go away,” he says. “All of you. In a minute. First, your homework.”

“Mr. Costigan,” Hale says, “that was very nearly an argument.” From Hale it lands like a medal pinned on with a thumbtack. Across the table Lena’s chin comes up and stays up. She writes something in red across the top of her syllabus and underlines it twice, hard enough that he hears the nib. She was owed this one, and the set of her mouth says she knows it.
“Mr. Costigan has won the room and lost the point,” Hale says. “He’ll go into politics.” The room laughs again — at Jack this time, which is a different sound. Lena doesn’t laugh.

“Miss Broussard has won,” Hale says. “Mr. Costigan has *attended*.” Lena doesn’t smile. She caps her fountain pen with one small precise click, like a woman who expected exactly this and was raised too well to enjoy it in public. Jack finds he doesn’t mind losing to her nearly as much as he ought to.

body: Hale stands, which is apparently the only warning they’ll ever get, and writes on the whiteboard in a hand like barbed wire.

body.title: PHIL 9H — the whiteboard
body.text:
TWO PAGES. EVERY WEEK.
Prove the thing you least believe you can prove.
Swap with your designated antagonist. Annotate each other in RED.
I grade the annotations.
Due at the start of class. Wednesday.

body: “The papers themselves,” he says, capping the marker, “I mostly use to level the dog’s bowl.” He pairs them off without looking at the roster. The Palo Alto girl with the chemistry kid. “Mr. Hargrove, Mr. Noorzai. Heaven help you both.” A deconvert with forty Post-its and a man nine hours into a fast regard each other across the oak. The San Diego boys with each other, “as a mercy.” “We’re not —” “I know.”
He doesn’t turn his head for the last one. “Mr. Costigan. Miss Broussard. You’ve already found each other.”

body.text: “I’m sure Mr. Costigan will be thorough,” Lena says — to Hale, not to Jack.
Nobody moves until Yusuf does. Then it’s chairs and bags and the door, early, and the room empties out around the oak. Lena stays in her seat a second longer than anyone, looking at the table.

journal.title: Designated antagonists
journal.text: Hale paired us. Two pages a week, swapped, bled on in red. For the whole semester. I’m going to need more pens.

s07.slug: MONDAY · 2:31 PM · HOLLIS HALL, CLOISTER WALK
body: On the cloister walk the heat comes up off the red tile as if it has been saving it. Across the Commons the Ferrer Tower’s carillon stumbles through the half hour, off-key, with the confidence of a man singing in the shower.

Caleb catches him at the arches, his book clutched to his chest. “He wrote you *back*? He knew the nine pages. I wrote him four letters. *Four.* I used a thesaurus on the third one. He never —” He laughs, to show it’s funny. It doesn’t come off. “One line,” Jack says. “Mostly a dare.” Which is true, and no help, and he watches it not help.

Lena is two steps away under the next arch, her syllabus against her chest. She says nothing. Her hands are still. She’s watching a bee work the bougainvillea, and the carillon finishes, and nobody fills the space after it.

Yusuf saves them, passing with his backpack on one shoulder. “Costigan. Iftar at the Islamic Center on Mission, any night this month. You Catholics like a long meal. We start at sunset and end when the dates run out.” Then, dry as a forecast: “My dad’s plant is closing, by the way. NUMMI. Toyota announced it last Thursday.” He goes off to find a quiet stairwell for the midday prayer he sat through Hale to keep. Two sons of auto workers at one oak table: Jack notices it the way you notice somebody from your own parish in an airport.
Caleb trails after him. Then it’s the two of them.

body: Jack wakes because the room is blue: a cold laptop glow from Theo’s side of 412, the Grove still black in the window. Theo is sitting up against the headboard in sheets that cost more than the Silverado’s last transmission, earbuds in, a Criterion case open on the blanket: *The 400 Blows*. On the screen, small and black-and-white, a boy is running.

He runs along a fence, down through scrub, across a gray beach and into the edge of the sea, where there’s nowhere left to go. He turns in the shallows and looks straight into the camera, and the picture stops on his face and stays there, looking at Jack across eleven feet of dorm room and fifty years.

Theo thumbs out an earbud. “Couldn’t sleep.” “Is it for a class?” “It’s for a class. French cinema. Very rigorous. There’s a midterm.” This from a man who told the floor meeting he was undeclared “the way Switzerland is undeclared.” The RAZR says 4:10. Jack rolls toward the wall. The trackpad clicks, and somewhere in France the boy begins to run again.

At 8:40 Theo is fresh as a commercial for himself, hair wet, no sign on him that he has ever seen four in the morning. Passion Pit pours out of the iPhone dock — a falsetto chopped into bright pieces, a music box having the best day of its life — and Jack is at the sink with his good flannel, scrubbing. The Jell-O shot he tucked in the pocket “for later” on Saturday went through Sunday’s wash. Later has arrived: a lime-green stain over the pocket in the shape of a heart, if you’re generous, and the soap is making it more generous.
“That’s not a stain, Costigan,” Theo says. “That’s a corsage.” He tilts his head. “Or did the swan come back for the other eyebrow? Has the family released a statement?”

You’re Sloane.”

Theo is flawless, and terrifying. He perches on the desk, lets his whole face go bored in an expensive way, and says from an octave down inside his own indifference, “Tell me about your *philanthropy*, Delaney.” “Well, Sloane, I believe every child deserves — ” “That’s what the Kappas say.” Laney clutches her heart as if shot. Jack is cast as Whitney, a Kappa legacy from Atherton. “Whitney. Atherton. We summer.” “Where?” “Yes.” Laney points at him with her whole arm. “Oh, she’s *good*. I hate her.”

Sloane wants to know if Delaney knows her odds. Laney doesn’t blink. “A hundred and twenty girls through the door last fall, forty-nine bids. So forty-one percent — well, forty point eight three — ” She hears herself. The smile comes on like stadium lights. “Or whatever. I’m a Gemini.” For one second Theo stops being Sloane, and the two of them look at each other across 412: two people who perform for a living, catching each other at it, delighted. Then he’s Sloane again, examining a cuticle.

On her way out she takes Jack’s RAZR out of his hand without asking — “This is like holding a clam that gave up” — curses T9 in a very Christian way, texts herself, and hands it back. It buzzes before it reaches his pocket.

body: Sandoval Hall 1 is four hundred orange flip-down seats raked toward a stage, poured in 1971 by somebody who believed in concrete. It smells of coffee and sunscreen. Jack comes in at 9:31 and finds row M by finding her.

Lena has her boots up on the seat in front and a highlighter in her teeth. Her canvas tote — OCTAVIA BOOKS · NEW ORLEANS — is on the seat beside her. She watches him come down the row, looks at the tote, and moves it to the floor, which leaves an empty seat between them that is now nobody’s fault. Folded on top of her books is a square of black lace. The 12:10 at St. Brendan’s, he’d bet. “You’re late, Youngstown.” “I was at a sorority.” “At nine in the morning?” “It was a practice sorority.”

Onstage, Adrian Hale has no notes and no intention of clipping on the wireless mic; he holds it between two fingers like a cigarette and conducts with it. “Socrates,” he says, “barefoot, unwashed, not long from being put to death by his own city for asking exactly this sort of question, meets a young man named Euthyphro, who is so certain what the gods want that he’s turning in his own father for the death of a hired man. And Socrates — nobody’s fool and everybody’s nuisance — asks him one question. Write it down. Some of you will spend your lives running from it.” Four hundred eighteen-year-olds who came for a general-ed requirement go quiet without knowing why. “Is the good loved by the gods because it is good? Or is it good because the gods love it? Plato says ‘pious.’ I’m saying ‘good,’ because none of you know what pious means, and the ones who do are lying.”

Something black lands in the empty seat: Margot Lindqvist, oxblood boots, a manila folder on her knees labeled in block capitals THE COSTIGAN PROBLEM. PHIL 1 is her gen-ed. “I said I’d destroy you,” she says, at a volume that does not acknowledge the lecture. “I’m methodical.” At the top of the first page, in a small sharp hand, are his own words from the fourth-floor lounge at three in the morning. “‘And every father.’ I’ve been thinking about it for two days.” A look over the black frames. “I resent that.”

Lena leans past her and puts out a hand. “Lena. Broussard. Two-seventeen.” Margot shakes it once, like signing for a package. “Margot. Lindqvist. Three-oh-five. You’re the one who made the beans. The whole stairwell smelled like pork fat and the Counter-Reformation.” Her eyes drop to the folded lace and stay there. “You wear a *mantilla*. In 2009. At a public university.” “You wear all black every day of your life,” Lena says pleasantly. “We’re both telling people how to look at us.” “Mine says *don’t*.” “So does mine. Mine just says it in Spanish.” “Lena, I say this with love,” Margot says, flat as a diagnosis: “you’ve internalized a two-thousand-year-old men’s club and you call it a personality.”

Down on the stage Hale has gone after the other horn and is having a wonderful time. “If the good is good because God commands it, then God could command cruelty on Thursday and you’d all be kicking dogs by Friday. Ethics by tantrum. A toddler with thunderbolts, and the lot of you obliged to call him Father.” Four hundred people laugh. Jack feels it go through the hall like a draft, and past him, and on the far side of Margot, Lena has stopped highlighting.

She leans across Margot and whispers, fierce, as if the three of them were in a pew and the homily had gone wrong. “It’s a false choice, and he knows it. The good isn’t a rule God has to obey, and it isn’t something He makes up on a Thursday. It’s what He *is*. The commands come out of His nature like light off the sun. Aquinas, first part, question six. Neither horn.” Jack had the same answer half built in his head. She has built it, painted it and moved in.

Margot does not whisper. “Fine. The good is God’s nature. Lovely. And who tells you what God’s nature requires? Men. In Rome. In very good hats. So in practice your third horn is held by a hierarchy that won’t let a woman anywhere near the microphone.” A nod at the stage, where a man is waving one around. “You didn’t escape Euthyphro. You outsourced him.”

Lena opens her mouth, and closes it. Jack has known her since Saturday and has never seen that. She’ll have an answer by tomorrow — a long one, with citations — but she doesn’t have it now, and all three of them know it.

Margot writes something in the folder and underlines it twice. “You’re useful idiots for Christian nationalism. Both of you. Goldberg, *Kingdom Coming*, 2006 — look it up.” She caps the pen. “It’s actually sweet.”

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Possibly my friend.

response: “Catherine of Siena starved herself to death at thirty-three,” Margot says without looking up. “Rudolph Bell, *Holy Anorexia*, 1985. Your exemplar is an eating disorder with a feast day.”

Lena turns in her seat with her whole body, thrilled to be fighting on two fronts before ten in the morning. “Oh, *Margot*,” she says, the way you’d greet a cousin you’ve been dying to fight with all through the wedding Mass, and Jack sits between their elbows and watches a friendship begin in the form of a war.

From the stage, without looking up, Hale says into the mic, “The three of you in row M will stop flirting or start charging admission,” and four hundred heads turn around.

body: The 11 bus runs down Mission to the water, and Jack rides it with a résumé on his knee, printed on the good paper he bought for college applications: Cardinal Mooney ’09. Latin Club. Point guard. *Summer: St. Brigid’s grounds crew.* Under SKILLS, after a long war with himself, *Hardworking.* He would like to die.

The harbor at seven is sea lions barking off the floats like a bad night at the union hall, diesel and frying oil, the sun going down orange behind the breakwater. Inside the Anchor somebody feeds the jukebox a quarter and Otis Redding is sitting on the dock of the bay, which down here is less a song than a job description.

The chalkboard by the register says PIE OF THE DAY: BOYSENBERRY. Beside it hangs a second board, new, the chalk still bright: JACK’S RATINGS: MARIONBERRY 4/10. Gloria is counting the drawer, pencil through the gray bun, and doesn’t look up. “Four out of ten. Your friend said your name was Jack and you were leaving. Then you left. After her.” The drawer shuts. “What do you want, Jack?” He puts the résumé on the counter. She doesn’t look at that either.

response: That gets her to look up — a long gray look at the hair that needs cutting and the good paper and the plain fact of him standing there saying it. “Plain,” she says, the way somebody else would say *apple*.
“Four out of ten?” She slides the résumé back to him unread. “Hon, you’re hired. Dishwasher quit at six. Apron’s on the hook.”

choices.text: “I’m your quality control.”
response: “I’ve heard better lines from men who smelled like bait,” Gloria says, still counting. “I married one.”
“Four out of ten?” She slides the résumé back to him unread. “Hon, you’re hired. Dishwasher quit at six. Apron’s on the hook.”

response: Gloria very nearly smiles. It gets as far as the pencil: out of the bun, a look at the point, back in.
“Four out of ten?” She slides the résumé back to him unread. “Hon, you’re hired. Dishwasher quit at six. Apron’s on the hook.”

body: Eight dollars an hour, Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays, seven to one, a share of tips. Saturdays start the twelfth, Gloria said, already walking away: this weekend her nephew Hector is home from Fresno State, “and he owes me.”

By 9:40 the dish pit has taught Jack everything it knows, which is steam. The Hobart is a steel box with a hood that drops like a guillotine and a cycle that sounds like a car wash losing an argument; the spray nozzle bucks on its spring over the slop sink like something alive; his fingers have pruned to the second knuckle. Through the pass-through, from the jukebox, Patsy Cline is heartbroken in a key the Hobart keeps interrupting.

The man on the line said “Rudy” at seven and offered a wrist instead of a greasy hand. He’s somewhere in his forties and does everything slowly, which turns out not to be the same as slow: three tickets on the flattop at once and none of them burning. A rosary is tattooed around his left wrist, the beads gone soft and blue. A transistor over the grill has Vin Scully walking the Dodgers through the late innings, and a Louis L’Amour — *Flint*, its spine mended with masking tape — rides in Rudy’s apron pocket. He introduced the machine before anything else — “Hobart. Older than you, meaner than Gloria” — and by the second rack Jack was *mijo*.

Gloria sweeps through with an armload of plates, sets them in Jack’s window, and says to Rudy, as though Jack were something in the pie case: “Lattice-top. Pretty on top. Everything’s leaking underneath.” Rudy considers him over the grill. “Hm.” “I’m standing right here,” Jack says. “I know where you’re standing, hon,” Gloria says, leaving. “I hired you.”

He loads the next rack wrong. Rudy leans over without a word, turns two plates with two fingers so the water can get at them, and goes back to his burgers. “First time I washed dishes was at Soledad,” he says, the way you’d say where you went to high school. “Six years. Best job in the building — it’s warm, and nobody bothers the dish man.” He flips a patty. Nothing in his face asks Jack to do anything with that. Nothing in it is hiding, either.

journal.title: Rudy (the Anchor)
journal.text: Line cook. Rosary on his wrist, Vin Scully on the radio, Louis L’Amour in his apron. Did six years at Soledad. Says the dish pit is the best job in any building.

journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask.

response: Rudy flips a burger without looking at it. “My mother. Every other Sunday. Three buses from Oxnard.”

Jack turns the spray on the next rack harder than any rack has ever needed. Water drums off the plates onto his apron and his shoes and the rubber mat. Out of the corner of his eye he sees Rudy look at the rack, and then at him, and then back down at the grill. Rudy doesn’t say anything. On the radio Vin Scully says it’s a beautiful night for baseball, and somewhere it probably is.

response: Rudy laughs — a real one, from somewhere low down, like it had to climb a ladder to get out. “Best company in California, mijo. Ask Gloria.” From the floor, without breaking stride: “*Don’t* ask Gloria.”

response: Jack says nothing and works: two hours of racks and steam and the slop sink, which he will not describe to anyone as long as he lives. At eleven a grilled cheese comes across the pass on a plate he washed himself, cut corner to corner, unasked for. “You’ll do,” Rudy says, and turns the radio up a notch.

s10c.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:15 AM · THE ANCHOR, THE WHARF
body: He comes out the back door at 1:15 smelling of Hobart steam and boysenberry, his hands white and ridged as a washboard, eleven dollars of tip-share folded in his jeans, and reads the schedule in the bus shelter twice. The last 11 left at 12:30. Under the planks the sea lions are still arguing.

A rusted single-speed beach cruiser comes ticking up the wharf out of the dark, a dented wire basket on the front. Its rider is sun-dark and salt-haired, with a laundry bag over one shoulder and a skateboard strapped to the bag, and Jack knows him before he knows from where: the other end of Saturday’s mini-fridge.

“Boss.” One flip-flop comes down. “Bus quit at twelve-thirty. Nobody told you?” “Nobody told me.” “Nobody tells anybody. Rafi. Two-oh-four. I had you as fridge guy.” “Jack.” Rafi is on his way to his dad’s place, two blocks up, to do laundry — “dorm machines eat quarters and socks; my dad’s only eat socks.”

He takes in Jack’s pruned hands, gets off the bike and holds it out by the handlebars. “Take her. Till Christmas.” Jack starts to say he can’t. Rafi talks over him, courteous and final. “She’s called La Flaca. Not stolen. Abandoned. My abuela says there’s about a week’s difference.” Coaster brakes — pedal backward; he demonstrates — and a seat that tilts like a barber’s chair. Then he drops the skateboard on the planks and rolls off up the wharf, wheels rumbling over the boards. “No stress, boss,” floats back: the same thing he said on Saturday over the fridge.

So Jack rides three miles home along the harbor road on a bicycle named for being skinny. The water is on his left, black and breathing, and the moon hangs over it three nights short of full, lopsided and bright enough to throw his shadow across the road beside him, a long thin Jack on a long thin bike. The chain clanks. The basket rattles at every seam in the asphalt. Nobody is asking him to prove anything — not his soul, not his pie, not his margins — and at the Grove he stands on the pedals up the last hill and comes down the far side with his feet off them, the way he used to come down Glenwood Avenue at eleven, all the way to the bottom, not braking once.

s11.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:15 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH FLOOR LANDING
body: The padded envelope in his mailbox is in his mother’s careful Palmer loops. Inside, between two pieces of shirt cardboard: Rosie. Jack in crayon on a yellow beach under a palm tree the size of a skyscraper. Beside him Hannah Montana, in a bikini drawn with great modesty — it reaches her knees and has sleeves. In the sand a cross, an arrow, and JACKS CHURCH. He’ll tape it over his desk tonight. For now he holds it on his knee on the fourth-floor landing of the east stairwell, where the one bar lives, while somebody a floor down smokes a clove and the whole stairwell smells like a Christmas candle that has taken up crime.

His father answers, which never happens. He made it home last night. The guy in Flagstaff says hello; Jack lets him. Then there’s a pause with the garage in it — the space heater ticking though it’s September, the radio low on the workbench — and Frank says, as if he’s carried it across half the country looking for a place to set it down: “Good grip. Saturday.” The handshake. Jack looks at his own hand. “Thanks, Dad.” “How’s the pelican?”
He remembers. Of course he remembers. “She’s in my philosophy class.” A mile of silence, then two thousand more. “What’d I tell you. Costigans don’t get the easy ones.”

Behind his father the radio says the name before Frank does. WKBN: Jim Traficant walked out of federal prison this morning in Rochester, Minnesota, in a gray T-shirt and white knee socks and folded himself into a cab, and the whole Valley watched him do it. “They’re throwing him a party,” Frank says. “Twenty bucks a ticket. Skinny ties and bell-bottoms.” Not proud, exactly; next door to proud. “A crook. But he was our crook.” “He took bribes, Dad.” “He took them for *us*.” Jack opens his mouth, and Frank says, “Here’s your mother.”

“What did you have for dinner?” “Chicken.” “What kind of chicken?” “Dining hall.” “Jackie. Dining hall is where it happened to the chicken.” She has already told the whole school office he’s coming for Thanksgiving. “And the veil girl?” “Ma.” “I’m allowed to ask. I’m your mother, it’s in the Catechism.”

Then the click and fumble of the extension in Nonna’s room, three tries, EWTN murmuring behind her. “Giacomino.” It’s the voice she uses on saints who are running late. “Primo venerdì. This Friday. You go *and* you go” — which in Nonna means Mass and confession both — and she hangs up on herself by accident.

Gina gets hold of the kitchen phone long enough to say, in exactly the voice she texts in, flat and lowercase with no punctuation anywhere, “nonna thinks california is in mexico i didnt correct her bye,” and is gone.
Then it’s his father again, clearing his throat, which for Frank is the sound of a phone call ending. There’s just room, before he hangs up, to tell him about the Anchor.

choices.text: Tell him about the job.
choices.key: You told your father you’d taken a job washing dishes.
response: “I got a job, Dad. Washing dishes. A diner on the harbor, nights.” A long pause. He can hear the radio in it, and the space heater, and his father breathing. “Good,” Frank says. “Work.” Another pause. “Don’t let it eat the reading.” It’s the most his father has said about his future since the driveway.

choices.text: Don’t. He’d say you’re there to study — and he’d drive back out to say it.
response: So Jack doesn’t. He lets his father keep believing whatever lets him sleep, the same way his father keeps the guy in Flagstaff for his mother.

choices.text: “I’m interning in the restaurant industry.”
response: “Don’t get smart.” Frank lets it go. Jack lets it go. The job stays where it is, unsaid, a pan left in the sink to soak.

s11b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL, 4TH FLOOR LANDING
body: “You write your brother yet?” his father says, at the end. “Doing it now.” “He reads ’em twice.” And the line goes dead the way it always does with Frank, no goodbye, as though goodbye were a waste of long distance. Jack doesn’t go back to the room. He stays on the landing with a yellow pad against his knee, under a fluorescent tube that buzzes and flickers and refuses to die, and writes the way he always writes to Danny: fast, no drafts, before he can turn it into anything.

body.text:
Danny —

The ocean is real. It’s cold, which nobody tells you.

My roommate owns a silk robe and an espresso machine and I’m not allowed to touch either. The professor drinks at lunch and is better than his book, which I’m not telling him.

I wash dishes now, Tuesday Thursday Saturday, a machine called Hobart that hates me. The cook’s name is Rudy. He reads Louis L’Amour and calls me mijo.

There’s a girl from New Orleans in my seminar who argues like a prosecutor and wins like one.

Don’t. I know.

—the Professor
Under the signature, smaller, he adds: *P.S. Dad doesn’t know about the dishes.* He looks at that line for a while and leaves it.

body: He addresses the envelope from memory. He doesn’t seal it until he’s read the letter twice, the way Danny will. Then he presses the flap shut with the side of his fist and puts it in the inside pocket of Danny’s jacket, where it crackles when he breathes. Through the six-inch window the fog is coming in over the Grove. It’s nearly seven, and he has somewhere to be at eight.

s12.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:02 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, NEWMAN HOUSE LOUNGE
body: He chains La Flaca to the Newman house railing at 8:01, the letter to Danny crackling in the jacket’s inside pocket; he’ll mail it tomorrow. The lounge smells of burnt coffee: a plaid couch from 1994 that sags like a hammock, a ping-pong table with a dead net, a shelf of donated books — three copies of *Mere Christianity* and one *Da Vinci Code* wearing a Post-it in a hand like barbed wire: *Read CRITICALLY. —D. Fitch.* Fr. Osei’s rubber boots stand by the door, still damp, as if they’ve just stepped out of him.

At a folding table a girl is lettering a poster with her tongue between her teeth — NEWMAN WELCOME BBQ & BEACH CLEANUP — SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 19 — and the second B is listing badly to port. Sunburn along the part in her hair, a braid as thick as a bell rope, forearms that have done things to hay. She holds out a hand with marker on every knuckle. “Becca. Lindell. Coeur d’Alene, Idaho — it’s a lake, people think it’s a cheese. Homeschooled. Seven siblings. A ranch.” She regards the poster as though it has personally let her down. “I can butcher a deer, but I can’t letter a poster, so this is humbling.”

Joey Abruzzo is helping, which in Joey’s case means a Yankees cap, masking tape worn as a bracelet, and volume. “JACK. Jack, we’re making a *list*.” Becca mentions her roommate is coming, a nursing major from Spokane. Joey lowers the RSVP sheet. “I’m going to be a priest,” he says, with tremendous dignity. “Is she single? I’m asking for the *seating chart*.” “It’s a beach, Joey. There’s no seating chart.” Joey considers this. “Then what am I asking for?”

Becca puts a Sharpie in Jack’s hand. “You letter. You have very Catholic-school handwriting.” “You haven’t seen my handwriting.” “I can tell from how you stand.” So he does the second poster in the Palmer method the sisters put into his wrist, every capital leaning the same way, and Becca watches the S in SEPTEMBER come out right and makes a small sound of grief. Then, bent over the beach umbrella she has been failing to draw for ten minutes, not looking up: “Do you have a girlfriend?” Joey stops taping. Becca adds a stripe to the umbrella. “For the seating chart.”

journal.title: Becca (Newman)
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings. Can butcher a deer. Running the Sept 19 BBQ like a cattle drive. Asked if I had a girlfriend. For the seating chart.

choices.text: “Put me down.”
response: Becca writes JACK C. on the list in letters a little too neat. She adds a smiley face. Then she crosses out the smiley face, twice, which is worse than the smiley face. Joey says, “*Wow*.”

choices.text: “I work Saturday nights. The day, sure.”
response: “A working man,” Becca says, and gives him one short nod, a rancher’s nod. “My dad would like you.” She means it as information, not flirtation — he’s almost sure — which is somehow more alarming. She writes JACK C. (DAYS) and underlines DAYS.

choices.text: “Is there a seating chart?”
response: “There is now,” Becca says, and draws a rectangle on the back of the RSVP sheet with enormous authority. Joey leans in. “Put me next to anyone with a pulse and a rosary.” She writes JOEY in one corner, very small, as far from everyone as the paper allows.

s12a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE CONFESSIONAL
body: “My grandmother sent me,” Jack says at the closet door; it seems only fair to name the responsible party. “First Friday’s this week.” Osei nods gravely. “Then we are both under orders.” He goes in first. After a moment his voice says, “Come.”

It used to be a coat closet, and under the lemon polish there’s still an old smell of wool and mothballs, fifty years of winters Marisol never had. A kneeler with cracked maroon vinyl; a folding chair beside it, so you can choose. A linen screen on a wooden frame with a lamp behind it, so that Osei is a shape and not a face. Jack kneels. He always kneels. The chair creaks; there’s the small business of a man arranging a leg that doesn’t fold the way it used to; then just his breathing, unhurried, the patience of somebody who used to listen to chests for a living.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It’s been — ” He says how long. Then he talks.

The vinyl is cold through his jeans, and then it isn’t. He holds his own hands the way he has since he was seven, thumbs crossed. The St. Michael medal swings out of his collar when he leans in. On Ocean Road a car goes by with a song in it, and is gone. Behind the linen Osei says nothing; he listens the way the closet does, with the whole room. It takes as long as it takes.

When Jack is finished, the shape behind the screen leans closer. “God is not a customs officer, Jack,” Osei says. “He is not looking for what you failed to declare. He is waiting at the door with the car running.” For a penance, a decade of the rosary — “any decade; I am not particular, and neither is He” — “and call your grandmother. The sisters who taught me arithmetic in Kumasi were Italian. I know who outranks me.”

Jack says the Act of Contrition, every word where he left it. On the linen the shadow of a hand lifts. “God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself and sent the Holy Spirit among us for the forgiveness of sins; through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” “Amen.” “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.” “His mercy endures forever.”

In the courtyard the sprinkler is still hissing at the flower bed. Jack stands under the olive tree with his hands in his brother’s pockets and feels — *light* is the only word, and it’s the wrong word, and it’s the one there is. He couldn’t defend it in Hollis 302; Hale would have it in pieces in four minutes, and Lena would supply the article number. He doesn’t try. He stands in it a while.

He says the decade on La Flaca on the way home, a Hail Mary every few dozen turns of the pedals. On the eighth, by the Grove, a skunk walks out onto the bike path as if it has an appointment, and Jack swerves into the ice plant — *Holy Mary, Mother of God* — and the skunk, unbothered, finishes crossing at the stately pace of a monsignor in a procession. Jack picks up where he left off. He doesn’t lose count.

s12b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, FR. OSEI’S OFFICE
s12b.music: E.T. Mensah & the Tempos — “All for You”
body: Fr. Osei’s office is the size of a parking space, and he has filled it with sound: a silver stereo on the filing cabinet plays highlife at a volume the neighbors would have opinions about, horns as bright as new doorknobs, a guitar circling one figure like a man dancing with somebody’s aunt at a wedding. Books stacked sideways on books. A stethoscope on a hook, as though he might still be paged. One desk drawer stands open, and in it a framed photograph lies face down, felt backing to the ceiling. The chessboard sits on the blotter: an old wooden set, the white queen’s bishop chipped at the miter.

“E.T. Mensah and the Tempos,” Osei says, easing into his chair and the left leg out under the desk. “The king of highlife. My father played this record until you could read the newspaper through it.” He turns the board so the white pieces face Jack. “White moves first. I like to see what a man does with an advantage.” What Jack does with it is bring his queen out on the fourth move, like a guy starting something in a parking lot. “Ah,” says Osei, pleased. “Youngstown.” He plays slowly and wins slowly, and Jack has the strong impression he is being allowed to think it’s close.

Osei nods at the *Spe Salvi* in Jack’s back pocket, the holy card sticking out of it, so Jack tells him between moves: the theologian-pope, Regensburg, a man who writes as if you can keep up and won’t slow down if you can’t. Osei listens with his chin on his fist. “A shy man,” he says, “made to stand on a balcony. I like him for that.” He takes a knight. “And Youngstown. You told me it was sadder than Springsteen says. Better pierogi. I have been thinking about these pierogi for four days.” “Potato and cheese. Old ladies in church basements make nine thousand of them every Lent.” “And they are good?” “They’re the only reason the Valley still has a population.” Osei writes something on an envelope. Jack is fairly sure it says *pierogi*.

Osei moves a pawn and nods at the Carhartt hanging off the back of Jack’s chair, too big in the shoulders even with nobody in it. “That is a serious coat, for a place that isn’t cold.” “It’s my brother’s.” “He let you take it?” “He’s not using it right now.”

Jack takes the pawn. Then he’s talking: about Hale, who called him a spaniel in front of the whole seminar; about Theo’s espresso machine, which has its own typed sign and better health insurance than Frank; about the Hobart, which is possessed, and could Osei look into that, professionally; about Gloria, who rates human beings like pie. Osei laughs at the Hobart and the pie. After the fourth thing he turns a knight in his fingers a while, sets it down on a square that ends something, and says it once, mildly, without looking up. “When a man jokes that much, it is because the truth is heavy and he is carrying it alone.” On the stereo the trumpet climbs and climbs and doesn’t come down.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Said when a man jokes that much, the truth is heavy. I didn’t have a comeback.

choices.text: One more joke. “Is that a proverb, or did you make it up just now?”
response: Osei laughs from the belly, the glasses jumping on their cord. “In Kumasi we say a proverb is only a joke that has paid its taxes.” He moves his bishop. Mate in four. He folds his hands on his stomach and lets Jack find it.

choices.text: “Yeah.” Just that.
response: Osei doesn’t push. He resets the board, piece by piece. “Next Wednesday, then,” he says. “Bring your brother’s jacket. It plays better chess than you do.”

choices.text: Turn it around: “What happened to your leg, Father?”
response: Osei smiles, not offended in the least, as if Jack has finally made a move worth the board. “A long story,” he says. “You tell me yours, one day, and I’ll tell you mine.” Without looking, he closes the open drawer with his knee.

s12f.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:09 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, NEWMAN HOUSE HALLWAY
body: At the end of the hallway a door stands half open on a highlife guitar going around and around like it has nowhere better to be. Across from it, printer paper is taped to the coat-closet door: CONFESSIONS WED 8:00 — KNOCK. Underneath, in pencil, somebody has added *(gently)*.

Fr. Osei leans in his doorway, reading glasses on their cord, sleeves rolled, as if he has been expecting the next person and it happens to be Jack. “Mr. Costigan.” He tips his head at the closet door. Then, over his shoulder, at the chessboard on his desk, the pieces set up and waiting. “The box, or the board?” Jack came because an eighty-four-year-old woman in Ohio told him to. Nobody mentioned there’d be a choice.

choices.text: “The box.”
choices.key: You went to confession on Wednesday night.

body: Danny’s letter goes into the blue mailbox on Ocean Road with a tin clank, and Jack goes in out of the noon glare. St. Brendan’s is cool and smells of beeswax. Fifteen people in a church built for six hundred, scattered under the upside-down hull of the roof like survivors of a wreck who’d rather not crowd each other.

Mrs. Fitch, with a Tupperware of lemon bars on the pew beside her like a guest she brought. An old man with a cane, praying or asleep; at his age it may be the same skill. Becca from last night, fingers still blue from poster marker. And Kevin Tran in a navy quarter-zip, who has saved Jack a seat by laying his Bible on it, the spine gone soft, tabbed in four colors. “Saw you on the steps. Figured.”

Three rows up is Lena: the oatmeal cardigan over a yellow sundress, bare-headed, her hair twisted up with a pencil through it. Jack spends the entrance antiphon not looking at the back of her neck, and does about as well at it as he does at most things he attempts in church.

body.text: Last night is still on him: a lightness he couldn’t defend to anybody in Hollis Hall, and has stopped trying to. He keeps expecting it to wear off. It keeps not.
body.else: Through the open sacristy door Fr. Osei, halfway into a white chasuble, catches Jack’s eye and moves an invisible knight.

body: White, for Gregory the Great. Mrs. Fitch reads Colossians in a voice meant for a much fuller church: “…giving thanks to the Father, who has made you fit to share in the inheritance of the holy ones in light.” *Inheritance.* Jack hears it in Yorkshire-under-Oxford and has to look at his shoes.

Then Luke, and the boats. *Master, we have worked hard all night and have caught nothing* — a working man’s line, tired and put out and doing it anyway. The nets fill and tear. And Simon Peter goes down on his knees in all that thrashing silver and says: *Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.*

For the homily Osei comes down into the aisle with his weight on the good leg, like a man at a bus stop who has news. “Peter tells Jesus to go away because he is a sinner. Jesus does not argue with him. He gives him a job.” He lets it sit in the cool air. “And Gregory, whose day it is, did not want his job either. He begged the emperor to let him off. The emperor said no.” The laugh lines deepen. “In my experience, God also usually says no.” He sits. The homily was shorter than the Gospel.
Jack holds on to it through the Creed and the bells. It doesn’t get lighter. He doesn’t set it down.

Lena goes before the recessional with a Greek grammar under her arm, genuflecting fast, the cardigan sliding off one shoulder, and then she’s a shape in the bright doorway, and then she isn’t. “Greek at one,” Kevin murmurs. “Tuesday too.”

At Anacapa Commons Kevin goes through the salad bar like a pharmacist filling a prescription — grilled chicken, egg whites, spinach — and sighs at the waffle line. He takes a paper boat of fries “for morale” and doesn’t touch them.

His BlackBerry buzzes face-up on the tray: MẸ. He sits up straighter for a woman two hundred miles north. “Dạ, Mẹ. Dạ… dạ… dạ.” Then, smooth as a hotel front desk: “Con học rồi.” He hangs up. “Told her I already studied. Orgo. AP credit — she thinks it makes me a genius.” He spears an egg white. “The book’s still in the shrink-wrap. My sister’s at UOP, dental school. Tina. Four-point-oh. Flossed in the womb.” Jack looks at him. “Your sister.” Kevin grins, the big floor-meeting grin. “The ‘only child’ thing? Rhetorical.”

Then he points a forkful of egg white across the table. “Respectfully, bro. You stared at her through the whole Gospel on Sunday. Today you stared at her through *Colossians*, which nobody does. She has a boyfriend. It’s on her Facebook. Everybody checked.” “Everybody?” “Doug checked.” He chews. “I’m just saying. As your designated adult.”

Behind them Theo drifts past with a tray holding a single espresso and half a grapefruit, a man between engagements. “Tran.” “Vance.” Like two boxers touching gloves before the bell. Theo lifts the grapefruit to Jack in salute and keeps walking, and Kevin goes back to his chicken.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school — ‘only child’ was rhetorical. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese.

choices.text: Ask about his family.
response: “What are they like? Your parents.” Kevin sets his fork down, and for a second there’s no bit ready. “My parents came on a boat,” he says. “I don’t get to have a bad semester.”

Then it’s folded up and put away, and he’s leaning across the table with real urgency. “Wait. Does Ohio have In-N-Out?” “No.” “Then what do you people *eat*?” “Pierogi. Sorrow.” “Respectfully,” Kevin says, “that’s a cry for help.”

choices.text: Match his dad jokes: “Why did the pre-med cross the road?”
response: Kevin doesn’t blink. “To shadow a surgeon on the other side.” He lights up like a scoreboard. “What do you call a philosophy major in four years?” “Go on.” “*Waiter.*” “How many Thomists does it take to change a lightbulb?” “How many?” “*Distinguo.*” Kevin has no idea what it means and wheezes anyway, openly, both palms flat on the table.
They keep it up, two grown men being terrible on purpose, until the girl at the next table picks up her tray and her calculus and relocates to another zip code.

choices.text: “What’s with you and Theo?”
response: Kevin’s smile stays exactly where it was. “Nothing. Met him at the floor meeting. Same as you.” He pushes the paper boat of fries across the table. “You want these? I only take them for morale.”

body: Hollis 108 is a basement with one window, at exactly ankle height to the world, so the hour comes with a parade of feet: Keds, flip-flops, a dog that stops, considers the window, and moves on. Eighteen desks. Dry-erase marker and somebody’s orange.

The TA writes his name on the board in square capitals — EVAN MARSH — and under it, smaller: *office hours: when I’m not finishing.* He’s lanky and gray at the temples, though he can’t be much past thirty, with wire glasses and a stained tan Carhartt over the back of his chair. On the desk, a bike helmet and a pack of American Spirits, the yellow kind.

Jack knows him. It takes a second, and then it doesn’t take anything: the glasses, the gray, the bike. The man at the end of the Lighthouse driveway on Saturday night, smoking in the dark, watching the house and not going in. Evan Marsh takes attendance with his eyes, and they go over Jack the way they go over everybody: once, and on.

body.text: At 4:01 Lena stops dead in the doorway with a Greek grammar against her chest. Her face finds him and goes polite. “Mr. Costigan. You’re in *this* section.” A breath. “Of course you are.”
body.else: At 4:01 Lena stops dead in the doorway with a Greek grammar against her chest. “You’re in *this* section?” She shuts her eyes briefly, a woman taking up her schedule with a higher power. “Of course you’re in this section.”

body: She sits one desk away from him, which in a room of eighteen is a kind of diplomacy.

Evan sits on the front edge of the desk. “Professor Hale asked you to prove you have a soul.” Minnesota, flat and exact. “I want something harder. Suppose you found out tonight that you don’t. Kierkegaard says purity of heart is to will one thing — so tell me what your one thing is. What would it cost you?”

A girl by the window in a Marisol Surf hoodie says, going red, that she thinks she’d be relieved. Nobody keeping score. Evan doesn’t smile and doesn’t correct her. “That’s honest. Kierkegaard would say you just told me what you’re afraid of. Keep it.” She looks like somebody handed her a coat.

A Sigma Rho kid with his visor on backwards tips his chair onto two legs. “Nothing, bro. I’d still be me.” “Then nothing you’ve ever done was done by anybody,” Evan says pleasantly. “Your mother raised a complicated puddle. Serious people believe that. They don’t say *bro* while they believe it. They lose sleep.” The kid turns it over. “Thanks, man,” he says, and means it.

Lena doesn’t raise her hand. She waits until the room is quiet enough to deserve it, and then she answers like a closing argument, each sentence laid on the one before. “Everything I love would turn into chemistry. My mother’s kitchen. My brothers. The Saints. Receptors and salt. And here’s the problem: I’d still love it, exactly the same. Only it would be a fact about *me*, not about any of them. Love would be a climate I have, with nobody on the other end of it.” She sits back. “That’s what it would cost. Everybody.”

Evan’s eyes come to Jack. Jack hadn’t planned to say anything, and then he does, quietly, in the voice that comes out when there isn’t time to make it funny. “Everything I’ve done since I was sixteen would just be stuff a body did. Nobody to answer for it.” He hears it land in the low room and keeps going. “That sounds like relief. It isn’t.”
Evan looks at the two of them a second longer than he has looked at anybody, then turns back to the window girl and asks what exactly she meant by *score*.

At ten to five the Hollis steps are warm as a griddle and empty except for Evan, lighting an American Spirit off a Bic with his hand cupped against the wind off the Commons. Lena has gone back in for her pen.

journal.title: Evan Marsh (TA)
journal.text: Thursday section, Hollis 108. Kierkegaard. Kind to the scared ones, murder on the lazy ones. Smokes American Spirits. Rides a bike.

journal.title: The guy at the end of the driveway
journal.text: The guy at the end of the driveway is my TA.

choices.text: “I saw you Saturday. End of the driveway at the Lighthouse.”
choices.key: You told Evan you’d seen him at the end of the Lighthouse driveway.
response: Evan doesn’t look at him right away. He takes a pull on the cigarette and lets the smoke go — a pause long enough to smoke in, and he smokes in it. “I ride out that way,” he says. “I don’t go to parties. I’m twenty-nine.” Then, still to the Commons: “Who’d you go with?”
“My roommate dragged me.”
Evan nods. He asks nothing else. He grinds the cigarette out under his heel, clips on the helmet, and goes down to the rack, and Jack watches him ride off across the grass, upright and unhurried.

journal.text: The guy at the end of the driveway is my TA. Says he doesn’t go to parties. Asked who I went with. Nothing else.

response: Jack says nothing. Evan finishes the cigarette in no hurry at all. “Good answer in there,” he says — about the section, not looking at him. “Don’t get used to it.” He goes down to the rack and unlocks his bike.

choices.text: Bum a cigarette: “American Spirit. You *are* a grad student.”
response: Evan shakes one out without comment and lights it for him, the Bic cupped between both their hands against the wind. It burns slower than a Marlboro and tastes like burnt toast and good intentions. The two of them stand on the steps of a philosophy building smoking and saying nothing, which seems to be how Evan likes his company. “They’re not better for you,” he says finally. “People think they are.” Then he clips on the helmet and rides off across the grass.

s15.slug: THURSDAY · 5:05 PM · HOLLIS HALL, FRONT STEPS
body: By five the light over the Commons has gone long and gold, and past the lawn the sea has gone to hammered brass. The bougainvillea has been letting go on the Hollis steps all afternoon, so Jack sits in a drift of magenta like somebody a flower girl gave up on.

Lena comes out with her pen and sits two steps above him, because she likes the height. Yesterday, across Hale’s oak, they slid their pages at each other without eye contact, like a hostage exchange. This is the first he’s seen of what she did to his.

body.text: “Mr. Costigan.” She holds it out between two fingers. “Your paper.”
body.else: “Costigan.” She holds it out between two fingers. “Your paper. Brace yourself.”

body.title: “That Faith Is Not an Inheritance” — J. Costigan
body.text:
Professor Hale says my faith is an address. Fine: I was baptized at St. Brigid’s before I could object. But an inheritance is something you can refuse, and nobody refuses a thing they’ve never had to pick back up. Pascal tells the man who can’t believe to do what believers do — holy water, Masses — and belief will come: *cela vous abêtira*. Hale reads that as proof that faith is a habit. I read it as proof that faith is a decision you keep making with your knees until your head catches up. I didn’t stay because I was told to. I stayed because I tried the door.

IN RED, IN THE MARGINS —
beside “nobody refuses a thing they’ve never had to pick back up”: NO.
beside the Pascal: You quoted Pascal at me. I taught you Pascal on Sunday. *Cite me.*
under the last line: This sentence is lying and you know it.

body: He laughs out loud. “You quoted Pascal at me *once*.” “On the Lord’s Day, in front of God and a coffee urn. That’s a lecture. I’ll expect a footnote.” He reads his last line again, the one with the door in it, and finds he doesn’t want to fight her on it, which is worse than losing. From the way she watches him read, she knows it too.
He hands hers back.

body.title: “That the Body Is Not a Rental” — M. Broussard
body.text:
Descartes parked the body at the curb with the keys in it, and we act surprised that nobody brings it back with a full tank. Aquinas won’t let us off so easy: the soul is the form of the body, so there is no *me* standing safely behind my skin, lending it out. What is done to the body is done to the person, every time. That is why the Creed says the resurrection of the *body* and not of some tasteful vapor. The objection from injury — that a body can be broken and the person goes on — I will take up next week. For now: a thing that can be wounded is *someone*. Hotels don’t bleed.

IN RED, IN THE MARGINS, HIS HAND —
across the top: This is the best paragraph I’ve read this year. I hate it.
beside “I will take up next week”: Coward.
under “Hotels don’t bleed”: Okay, fine.
She reads his red aloud, perfectly courteous, like a hostess reading out a toast somebody else wrote.
body.else: She reads his red aloud in her Ohio voice, the flat one she’s been working on since Saturday.

body: “‘This is the best paragraph I’ve read this year. I hate it.’ It’s the third of September.” “It’s been a long year.” “And *coward*? Next to my deferral?” “It was a deferral.” “It was a *promise*. I keep mine.” She finds *Okay, fine* under her last line and doesn’t read that one aloud. She looks at it for a while, though, with the pen between her teeth.

Down on the Commons a dog goes after a Frisbee with its entire life. Lena folds her paper in half, creases it with a thumbnail, and says, to the sea more than to him: “You heard me Sunday. On the stairs.”
“Medals off,” Jack says.

She almost smiles. “I don’t like a thing sitting on a table between two people where nobody will touch it. It goes bad.” She holds the folded paper flat on her knees against the breeze. “His name is Wes. Wesley Arceneaux. Tulane, civil engineering. He wants to build the walls right.” She says *the walls* the way Jack’s father says *the plant*, as if there has only ever been the one.

s17a.slug: FRIDAY · 7:31 PM · SEACLIFF ROAD, PI LAMBDA CHI
body: Seacliff Road at dusk is jasmine on the fences and the sea loud at the end of every cross street, and behind them, over the brown hills, the moon is coming up full and enormous, the color of a peach left on a windowsill. Laney walks between them in a white strapless dress she and Lena ironed last night, badly, which is why a wide braided belt rides low over the scorched triangle on her left hip. “Nobody look at my hip.” Nobody can stop.
